You are in /home/user/fortress, a git repo reviving Sun's Fortress language. Commit 8fe1daa8f ("Import pluckyporcupine's Scala 2.10.7 / Java 9 migration as a tree overlay") grafted a third party's modernization onto Sun's 2012 tree (parent commit a874948ac). We already know one blunder in that graft: to fix a JDK-9-encapsulated import `com.sun.org.apache.bcel.internal.generic.INVOKEINTERFACE` in MethodInstantiater.java — an import that was DEAD CODE (unused) — porcupine vendored the entire Apache BCEL source tree (378 files, ProjectFortress/src/org/apache/bcel/) plus a bcel.jar, instead of deleting one line.

Your task: audit the ENTIRE graft diff for other mistakes of this kind, and characterize everything it changed. Be thorough — this audit decides whether we rebuild our history on a corrected base.

Method suggestions (very thorough):
- `git diff --stat a874948ac 8fe1daa8f` is huge; start with `git diff --stat a874948ac 8fe1daa8f | tail -40` for totals and `git diff --name-status a874948ac 8fe1daa8f | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c` for add/delete/modify counts.
- Categorize ADDED files (A): vendored third-party code, junk/scratch files (compile_errors*.txt, logs, IDE droppings, .DS_Store), build artifacts, legitimately new build files (third_party/ jars), READMEs.
- Categorize DELETED files (D): did porcupine delete anything from Sun's tree (tests, docs, code)? List every deletion — deletions from the historical artifact matter most.
- For MODIFIED files: bucket them. `git diff a874948ac 8fe1daa8f -- <path>` on samples from each bucket. Expected legitimate buckets: Scala 2.8→2.10 API migration in ProjectFortress/src/scala_src (e.g. deprecated methods), build.xml rewrite, Java 9 compatibility fixes. Look for anti-patterns: wholesale reformatting / line-ending churn masking real changes, commented-out code instead of fixes, deleted assertions or tests weakened to pass, changes that "fix" errors by removing functionality, encoding damage (mojibake), copyright header removal, sloppy find-replace damage.
- Specifically check: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/useful/MagicNumbers.java mentions "bcel" — why? Root LICENSE mentions bcel — what did porcupine do to LICENSE? ProjectFortress/.dependencies/dependencies.txt — what is it? compile_errors*.txt (1-4) at repo root — confirm they are porcupine's scratch logs.
- Check what happened to Sun's third-party arrangement: parent tree had no ProjectFortress/third_party — where did Sun keep jars, and how did porcupine restructure that?
- Count how many modified files are pure whitespace/line-ending changes vs substantive: for a sample, `git diff -w --stat a874948ac 8fe1daa8f -- <file>`.

Return a structured report: (1) diff totals by A/M/D; (2) deletions list with assessment (was anything of value destroyed?); (3) additions categorized, flagging junk; (4) modification buckets with counts, sample evidence per bucket, and any anti-patterns found — each with file paths and a 1-2 line evidence quote; (5) a verdict: which parts of the graft are sound migration work worth keeping, which parts are mistakes to correct if we rebuilt history on a corrected base. Raw data over polish; file paths everywhere.

# FORTRESS

This is an effort to update Sun's Fortress programming language to work on Java 9 and, later, Java 10. As of 03/26/2018, the interpreter is running and all Java warnings have been cleared. The compiler works, but running compiled programs does not.

## Important notes:

- The version used for this is not quite the final version. Instead, the version used was cloned from a commit made on June 12th, 2012, as later versions threw errors at runtime.
- The original readme file, which includes basic instructions for compiling and running Fortress, as well as setting up the Emacs and Vim script files, is named README.txt and can be found in the base directory of this repository.

## Confirmed working on:

| Platform    | x86 (Java 9)  | x86_64 (Java 9)   | x86 (Java 10) | x86_64 (Java 10)  |

### Bucket E — `FTypeTuple` / `FTypeArrayList` (1 modified + 1 added) — ANTI-PATTERN, the second-worst call in the graft

`/home/user/fortress/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/types/FTypeTuple.java`:
```java
      TreeSet<List<FType>> s = new TreeSet<List<FType>>();
-     s.add(Collections.<FType>emptyList());
+     s.add(new FTypeArrayList());
...
-     ArrayList<FType> a = new ArrayList<FType>();
+     FTypeArrayList a = new FTypeArrayList();
```

The real defect: a comparator-less `TreeSet` requires `Comparable` elements, and JDK 7+ `TreeMap.put` calls `compare(key,key)` on the *first* insert, so Sun's latent bug started throwing `ClassCastException`. The correct fix was one line — the repo already ships the exact tool:
`/home/user/fortress/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/useful/ListComparer.java` (a `Comparator<List<T>>`, extending `AnyListComparer`), i.e. `new TreeSet<List<FType>>(new ListComparer<FType>())`.

Instead porcupine added a new class whose `Comparable` implementation is a stub:
```java
public class FTypeArrayList extends ArrayList<FType> implements Comparable {
  @Override
  public int compareTo(Object o) {
    return 0;          // ← every instance compares equal to every other
  }
```
Any `TreeSet<FTypeArrayList>` silently collapses to at most **one** element. This is a "make the exception go away" fix that trades a loud crash for silent wrong answers in interpreter type meet/join.

Mitigating (I traced it): the blast radius is currently bounded, because `Useful.setProduct` (`/home/user/fortress/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/useful/Useful.java:262`) returns a `HashSet` and rebuilds plain `ArrayList`s, so the poisoned `TreeSet` only ever holds the single seed element before being discarded. So it's a **landmine, not an active corruption** — but it's exactly the kind of landmine that detonates the moment someone reuses `FTypeArrayList` or fixes `setProduct`.

- Its `compareElements` anonymous `Comparator<FType>` is a **verbatim copy-paste** of `ListComparer`'s inner comparator, comment included (*"Deal appropriately with null, which for convenience we consider to be less than everything else."*).
